claims.text: Thermal pre-treatment of FeNiCrCoCu will cause Cu to segregate selectively to the near-surface region.
The segregated Cu will preferentially oxidize into a continuous, adherent, Cu-rich oxide layer.
Thermal pre-treatment will refine the grain structure beneath the FeNiCrCoCu surface.
The Cu-rich oxide layer and refined subsurface grains will act synergistically to impede crack initiation and reduce high-temperature wear.
The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating has a relatively coarse, homogeneous nanocrystalline structure.
The as-deposited coating has no preferential surface oxidation.
The proposed intervention is annealing at approximately 500°C for one hour in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere with controlled oxygen partial pressure.
Adjusting oxygen partial pressure during the 500°C anneal can favor selective Cu oxidation while suppressing oxidation of the other alloy elements.
The proposed wear test is conducted at approximately 600°C and a normal load of 10 N under controlled sliding conditions.
Annealing-enhanced atomic mobility will drive Cu toward the surface and enable its preferential oxidation.
A dense oxide layer can reduce direct asperity contact and delay oxidation-induced coating breakdown.
Grain refinement increases local hardness and resistance to crack initiation.
The pre-treated coating will contain a continuous Cu-rich oxide layer detectable by SEM, EDS, and XRD.
The pre-treated coating will exhibit a refined nanocrystalline near-surface structure.
At 600°C, the pre-treated coating will have a lower friction coefficient than the untreated coating.
At 600°C, the pre-treated coating will have a significantly lower wear rate than the untreated coating.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply primarily near 600°C and a 10 N normal load, while other degradation mechanisms may dominate outside that regime.
Copper oxides may have inadequate long-term stability or adhesion at high temperature.
Deviation from the optimized annealing conditions may oxidize other alloy elements and compromise wear resistance.
Absence of the proposed microstructural changes or absence of a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear relative to the untreated control will falsify the hypothesis.
